segments.narration: Narrate: 'A sharp corner, built from nothing but smooth curves — how is that possible?' Show a square wave drawn in bold, then overlay a single sine wave beneath it. The gap between them is the question.

Start with just one sine wave — it captures the rough shape, a single smooth hump per half-period, but it misses those sharp edges completely. Now add a second wave, sin of three x, at one-third the amplitude. Watch the sum: the top flattens, the sides steepen, and the gap to the square wave visibly shrinks.
Each new wave has a higher frequency and smaller amplitude — sin of 3x over 3, then sin of 5x over 5, and so on. Watch the edges sharpen as we stack more harmonics onto the square wave.

Each term follows a clear rule: only odd frequencies, and each amplitude is exactly one over n. Sin of x over 1, sin of 3x over 3, sin of 5x over 5 — the pattern keeps going, always odd n, always shrinking by that same factor.

Narrate: 'Any periodic function can be written as an infinite sum like this.' Display the Fourier series formula. Point to each part — the coefficients a_n and b_n — and link them visually back to the amplitudes already on screen.

To find each coefficient b_n, multiply the target function by sin of n x and average over one cycle. Watch what happens: when the frequency matches, the product is always positive, so the area is a real nonzero number. But when the frequency does not match, the positive and negative regions cancel perfectly — the integral collapses to zero.

Even with infinitely many terms, there is a permanent nine percent overshoot right at the jump. The series converges everywhere, but not uniformly — that spike shrinks but never fully disappears, and this is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

And there we have it — any periodic shape is secretly a recipe, a list of frequencies and their amplitudes. Fourier series make that recipe readable. We started with a jagged square wave that seemed impossible to build from smooth curves, and now we see exactly how it is done.
